claim: The smooth eye movement region of the frontal eye fields (FEFSEM) is a critical node in the neural circuit controlling smooth pursuit eye movement.
source: The smooth eye movement region of the frontal eye fields (FEFSEM) is a critical node in the neural circuit controlling smooth pursuit eye movement.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work throughout the manuscript showing effects of lesions and inactivation.

claim: Preparatory activity evolves in the monkey FEFSEM during fixation in parallel with an objective measure of visual-motor gain.
source: Preparatory activity evolves in the monkey FEFSEM during fixation in parallel with an objective measure of visual-motor gain.
evidence: This claim is supported by the parallel time courses shown in Figure 2 comparing neural preparatory activity and behavioral measures of visual-motor gain.

claim: The use of FEFSEM output as a gain signal rather than a movement command allows for preparation to progress in pursuit without causing movement.
source: We propose that the use of FEFSEM output as a gain signal rather than a movement command allows for preparation to progress in pursuit without causing movement.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their data showing parallel progression of preparatory activity and gain modulation.

claim: Preparatory modulation of firing rate in FEFSEM predicts movement.
source: We also show that preparatory modulation of firing rate in FEFSEM predicts movement, providing evidence against the 'movement-null' space hypothesis as an explanation of how preparatory activity can progress without movement.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the optimal linear model analysis in Figures 5 and 6 showing that preparatory activity projects onto movement-potent dimensions.

claim: There is a partial reorganization of FEFSEM population activity between preparation and movement.
source: Finally, there is a partial reorganization of FEFSEM population activity between preparation and movement that would allow for a directionally non-specific component of preparatory visual-motor gain enhancement in pursuit.
evidence: This is supported by the principal component analysis in Figure 7 showing that the angle between preparatory and pursuit principal components is neither 0 nor 90 degrees.

claim: Inactivation or lesioning of FEFSEM produces dramatic defects in smooth pursuit.
source: Inactivation or lesioning of FEFSEM produces dramatic defects in smooth pursuit (Keating, 1991; Shi et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Micro-stimulation of FEFSEM induces smooth eye movement.
source: Micro-stimulation induces smooth eye movement (Gottlieb et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Strong modulation of activity in FEFSEM occurs just before the initiation of pursuit.
source: Strong modulation of activity occurs just before the initiation of pursuit (MacAvoy et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The modulation of FEFSEM activity is tuned for the direction of visual motion and eye movement and is monotonically related to their speeds.
source: The modulation is tuned for the direction of visual motion and eye movement and is monotonically related to their speeds (Gottlieb et al., 1994; Tanaka and Lisberger, 2002a; Tanaka and Lisberger, 2002b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: FEFSEM cells show an impressive ramp increase in firing rate during fixation, at a time when there is neither visual motion nor smooth eye movement.
source: Importantly, the same cells that discharge in relation to the initiation of pursuit also show an impressive ramp increase in firing rate during fixation, at a time when there is neither visual motion nor smooth eye movement (Mahaffy and Krauzlis, 2011; Tanaka and Fukushima, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is also demonstrated in the current data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Preparatory activity in FEFSEM grows over the hundreds of milliseconds preceding visual motion and the onset of pursuit.
source: The preparatory activity grows over the hundreds of milliseconds preceding visual motion and the onset of pursuit, and its amplitude encodes expectation of upcoming target speed and combines with visual-motion input in a reliability-weighted manner to determine pursuit-related responses (Darlington et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the same authors and is demonstrated in the current data in Figure 2C.

claim: The amplitude of preparatory activity in FEFSEM encodes expectation of upcoming target speed.
source: The preparatory activity grows over the hundreds of milliseconds preceding visual motion and the onset of pursuit, and its amplitude encodes expectation of upcoming target speed and combines with visual-motion input in a reliability-weighted manner to determine pursuit-related responses (Darlington et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and is demonstrated in the current data in Figure 3B.

claim: In the arm movement system, populations of neurons act as a dynamical system in which preparatory activity sets the initial conditions for the progression of movement activity.
source: In the arm movement system, the current paradigm suggests that populations of neurons act as a dynamical system in which preparatory activity sets the initial conditions for the progression of movement activity (Churchland et al., 2010; Churchland et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the arm movement system.

claim: Preparatory population activity in primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) progresses in a way that avoids dimensions related to movement.
source: Importantly, preparatory population activity in primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) progresses in a way that avoids dimensions related to movement (Kaufman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work in the arm movement system.

claim: Preparatory activity in M1 and PMd remains confined to 'movement-null' dimensions until just before movement initiation.
source: It remains confined to 'movement-null' dimensions until just before movement initiation, and only then begins to progress along 'movement-potent' dimensions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the context of citations to prior work on the arm movement system.

claim: The preparatory and movement-related population responses in M1 and PMd occupy orthogonal dimensions.
source: Indeed, the preparatory and movement-related population responses in M1 and PMd occupy orthogonal dimensions (Elsayed et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work in the arm movement system.

claim: The use of output-null neural dimensions plays a role in M1's initial processing of visuomotor feedback during movement.
source: Furthermore, the use of output-null neural dimensions plays a role in both M1's initial processing of visuomotor feedback during movement as well as short-term force-field adaptation in PMd (Perich et al., 2018; Stavisky et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The use of output-null neural dimensions plays a role in short-term force-field adaptation in PMd.
source: Furthermore, the use of output-null neural dimensions plays a role in both M1's initial processing of visuomotor feedback during movement as well as short-term force-field adaptation in PMd (Perich et al., 2018; Stavisky et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the saccadic eye movement system, movement is prevented during preparation via the action of an all-or-none inhibitory gate created by the action of omnipause neurons in the brainstem.
source: In the saccadic eye movement system, movement is prevented during preparation via the action of an all-or-none inhibitory gate created by the action of omnipause neurons in the brainstem (Cohen and Henn, 1972; Keller, 1974; Luschei and Fuchs, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the saccadic system.

claim: Ramps of preparatory activity in the saccadic region of the frontal eye fields fail to trigger eye movements until the collective descending activity from the frontal eye fields and superior colliculus cause the omnipause neurons to cease firing.
source: Ramps of preparatory activity in the saccadic region of the frontal eye fields fail to trigger eye movements until the collective descending activity from the frontal eye fields and superior colliculus cause the omnipause neurons to cease firing, releasing the circuits that generate movement (Dorris et al., 1997; Hanes and Schall, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the saccadic system.

claim: Subthreshold activity in the superior colliculus possesses some motor potential when omnipause neurons are inhibited by the trigeminal blink reflex.
source: Furthermore, subthreshold activity in the superior colliculus possesses some motor potential when omnipause neurons are inhibited by the trigeminal blink reflex (Jagadisan and Gandhi, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: There is no evidence that the pursuit system uses the all-or-none gate that controls saccades.
source: However, there is no evidence that the pursuit system uses the all-or-none gate that controls saccades (Missal and Keller, 2002; Schwartz and Lisberger, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work showing differences in omnipause neuron behavior during pursuit versus saccades.

claim: The outputs from the FEFSEM seem to control the gain of visual-motor transmission for pursuit.
source: The outputs from the FEFSEM seem to control the gain of visual-motor transmission for pursuit (Nuding et al., 2009; Tanaka and Lisberger, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Visual-motor gain is dialed up in preparation for an imminent smooth eye movement.
source: Further, visual-motor gain is dialed up in preparation for an imminent smooth eye movement (Kodaka and Kawano, 2003; Tabata et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is demonstrated in the current behavioral data in Figure 2B.

claim: There is a positive relationship between preparatory- and pursuit-related firing rate modulation across the FEFSEM population.
source: We observed a wide range of preparatory- and pursuit-related firing rate modulation across our FEFSEM population, and there was a positive relationship between preparatory- and pursuit-related firing rate modulation (Figure 1D, Monkey Re: Spearman's correlation coefficient = 0.17, p=0.02, n = 187 data points from 80 neurons; Monkey Xt: Spearman's correlation coefficient = 0.55, p=4.5×10−10, n = 110 data points from 66 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the neural data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Eye velocity responses to visual motion pulses during fixation were larger at later fixation times.
source: Figure 2A illustrates data from one example session showing larger eye speed responses at later fixation times in response to identical, but differently-timed, pulses of visual motion.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The behavioral assessment of visual-motor gain increases as a function of fixation time.
source: The behavioral assessment of visual-motor gain increases as a function of fixation time, paralleling the progression of preparatory activity in FEFSEM.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Modulation of FEFSEM preparatory activity showed a very similar time course across fixation for the overwhelming majority of neurons that had positive preparatory firing rate modulation.
source: Modulation of FEFSEM preparatory activity showed a very similar time course across fixation for the overwhelming majority of neurons that had positive preparatory firing rate modulation (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the neural data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a positive correlation between neural preparatory responses and behavioral measures of visual-motor gain across the population of neurons.
source: We can see the tight link between visual-motor gain and preparatory firing if we plot the behavioral results from Figure 2B against the preparatory firing from Figure 2C for each fixation time and each monkey (Figure 2D). The relationship is fairly linear with a positive correlation between neural responses and behavior across our population of neurons (slopes were computed for each neuron using linear regression: monkey Re mean = 0.073 degrees/spike, p=2.34×10−11, n = 135 data points from 66 neurons monkey Xt mean = 0.074 degrees/spike, p=2.76×10−11, n = 67 data points from 45 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the relationship between neural and behavioral data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The amplitude of FEFSEM preparatory activity encodes an expectation of target speed based on experience in blocks of trials with different blends of target speed.
source: We showed previously that the amplitude of FEFSEM preparatory activity encodes an expectation of target speed based on experience in blocks of 50 trials with different blends of target speed (Figure 3A; Darlington et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and is demonstrated in the current data in Figure 3B.

claim: Preparatory firing rate modulation was larger in magnitude during the 'fast-context' compared to during the 'slow-context'.
source: Preparatory firing rate modulation was larger in magnitude (Figure 3B) during the 'fast-context' (green traces, 80% of trials at 20 deg/s and 20% at 10 deg/s) compared to during the 'slow-context' (blue traces, with 80% of trials at 2 deg/s and 20% at 10 deg/s).
evidence: This claim is supported by the neural data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Visual-motor gain during the preparatory period is enhanced in the fast context compared to the slow context.
source: Based on behavioral assessment using pulses of visual motion during fixation, visual-motor gain during the preparatory period also is enhanced in the fast context compared to the slow context.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: In the fast-context versus slow-context, the mean eye velocity responses to the pulse were 3.02 ± 0.71 deg/s (SD) versus 2.27 ± 0.73 deg/s (SD), and the difference was statistically significant.
source: In the fast-context versus slow-context, the mean eye velocity responses to the pulse were 3.02 ± 0.71 deg/s (SD) versus 2.27 ± 0.73 deg/s (SD), and the difference was statistically significant (p=8.30×10−6, paired, two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 26 behavioral experiments in two monkeys, z = 4.46, Cohen's d = 1.06).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Eye speed responses were largest for same-direction pulses, intermediate for orthogonal-direction pulses, and smallest for opposite-direction pulses.
source: Across the full duration of fixation, eye speed responses were largest for same-direction pulses, intermediate for orthogonal-direction pulses, and smallest for opposite-direction pulses (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For all directions, eye speed responses increased as a function of time during fixation for same-, orthogonal-, and opposite-direction pulses.
source: For all directions, eye speed responses increased as a function of time during fixation for same-, orthogonal-, and opposite-direction pulses.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 4A and the statistical analysis provided in the text.

claim: For the same direction, orthogonal direction, and opposite direction pulses, the mean (+/- S.D.) slopes across 30 experiments in two monkeys were 1.05 ± 0.59 deg/s per s, 0.73 ± 0.40 deg/s per s, and 0.72 ± 0.45 deg/s per s.
source: We quantified the effect of fixation time by computing the slope of response amplitudes across pulse times. For the same direction, orthogonal direction, and opposite direction pulses, the mean (+/- S.D.) slopes across 30 experiments in two monkeys were 1.05 ± 0.59 deg/s per s, 0.73 ± 0.40 deg/s per s, and 0.72 ± 0.45 deg/s per s.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: The effect of fixation time on response amplitude was significant across all directions.
source: The effect of fixation time on response amplitude was significant across all directions using 2-sided Wilcoxon signed rank tests: same-direction (p=2.60×106, z = 4.70); orthogonal-direction (p=1.73×10−6, z = 4.78); and opposite-direction (p=4.78×10−6, z = 4.78).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: The differences in eye speed responses between same-direction and orthogonal-direction pulses were statistically significant.
source: The differences from same-direction were statistically significant using the paired sample, 2-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test for n = 30 experiments on two monkeys: same versus orthogonal-pulses (p=0.0093, z = 2.60, Cohen's d = 0.63); same- versus opposite-direction pulses (p=0.029, n = 30, z = 2.19, Cohen's d = 0.62).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: There is a greater preparatory enhancement of visual-motor gain in the expected direction of the upcoming pursuit trial.
source: Thus, there is a greater preparatory enhancement of visual-motor gain in the expected direction of the upcoming pursuit trial.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing larger responses to same-direction pulses compared to orthogonal and opposite-direction pulses.

claim: The increase in response amplitude over fixation time for all directions of pulses indicates a degree of directionally non-specific preparatory enhancement of visual motor gain.
source: Further, the increase in response amplitude over fixation time for all directions of pulses indicates a degree of directionally non-specific preparatory enhancement of visual motor gain.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing increases in responses to all pulse directions over fixation time.

claim: FEFSEM neurons display the largest modulation of firing rate during fixations leading to target motion towards their preferred direction.
source: Consistent with a larger behavioral preparatory enhancement of visual-motor gain in the expected direction, FEFSEM neurons display the largest modulation of firing rate during fixations leading to target motion towards their preferred direction (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the neural data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Preparatory firing rate modulation was smallest for upcoming target motions that were opposite to the preferred direction and intermediate for upcoming target motions that were orthogonal to the preferred direction.
source: Preparatory firing rate modulation was smallest for upcoming target motions that were opposite to the preferred direction and intermediate for upcoming target motions that were orthogonal to the preferred direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the neural data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The first three components obtained via dPCA account for ~90% of the variance of the FEFSEM population preparatory response.
source: The first three components obtained via dPCA account for ~90% of the variance of our FEFSEM population preparatory response (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the dPCA analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Component one from dPCA is direction-independent.
source: Component one is direction-independent.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dPCA analysis shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: The projections of FEFSEM preparatory population activity onto component one both increase across fixation for impending target motion toward and away from the preferred direction.
source: The projections of FEFSEM preparatory population activity onto component one both increase across fixation for impending target motion toward and away from the preferred direction (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the dPCA analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The projections onto component one are consistent with the directionally nonspecific enhancement of visual-motor gain observed for the orthogonal and opposite-direction visual motion pulses.
source: The projections onto component one are consistent with the directionally nonspecific enhancement of visual-motor gain observed for the orthogonal and opposite-direction visual motion pulses.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation linking the neural dPCA results to the behavioral findings.

claim: Component two from dPCA is direction-dependent.
source: Component two is direction-dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dPCA analysis shown in Figure 4C and 4E.

claim: The projections of FEFSEM population activity onto component two are offset from each other with the projections for toward and away motion sitting above and below each other, respectively.
source: (i) The projections are offset from each other with the projections for toward and away motion sitting above and below each other, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dPCA analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The offset between the projections onto component two is consistent with the behavioral finding of an offset between the eye speed responses to brief target motions in the same versus opposite direction from expected target motion.
source: The offset between the projections is consistent with the behavioral finding of an offset between the eye speed responses to brief target motions in the same versus opposite direction from expected target motion: there is a substantial difference in eye speed responses to the same and opposite visual motion pulses even at the earliest fixation times we tested.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation linking the neural dPCA results to the behavioral findings.

claim: The projection for motion toward the preferred direction increases and that for motion away from preferred projection decreases during the latter half of the fixation period for component two.
source: (ii) The projection for motion toward the preferred direction increases and that for motion away from preferred projection decreases during the latter half of the fixation period.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dPCA analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Component three from dPCA is direction dependent.
source: Component three also is direction dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dPCA analysis shown in Figure 4C and 4F.

claim: The projection of FEFSEM population activity onto component three shows a ramp increase for impending target motion toward the preferred direction and a ramp decrease for impending target motion away from the preferred direction.
source: The projection of FEFSEM population activity onto component three also shows a ramp increase for impending target motion toward the preferred direction and a ramp decrease for impending target motion away from the preferred direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dPCA analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The increase and decrease of the projections onto components 2 and 3 are consistent with the larger enhancement of visual-motor gain across fixation time for the same versus opposite direction visual motion pulses.
source: The increase and decrease of the projections onto components 2 and 3 are consistent with the larger enhancement of visual-motor gain across fixation time for the same versus opposite direction visual motion pulses.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation linking the neural dPCA results to the behavioral findings.

claim: The neural basis for the behavioral preparatory enhancement of visual-motor gain can be fully reconstructed from the first 3 dPCA components of the FEFSEM preparatory population response.
source: In conclusion, the neural basis for the behavioral preparatory enhancement of visual-motor gain can be fully reconstructed from the first 3 dPCA components of the FEFSEM preparatory population response.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the dPCA analysis and its relationship to the behavioral data.

claim: Studies of arm movement have shown that population preparatory activity in M1 and PMd evolves in a manner that does not predict movement.
source: Studies of arm movement have shown that population preparatory activity in M1 and PMd evolves in a manner that does not predict movement (Kaufman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work in the arm movement system.

claim: Movement is prevented during preparation in M1 and PMd because the population activity resides in 'movement-null' neural dimensions.
source: Movement is prevented during preparation because the population activity resides in 'movement-null' neural dimensions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the context of citations to prior work on the arm movement system.

claim: Humans and monkeys can initiate smooth pursuit in the absence of visual motion under certain conditions.
source: A priori, such a mechanism could generalize to the smooth pursuit eye movement system, especially since humans and monkeys can initiate smooth pursuit in the absence of visual motion under certain conditions (Freyberg and Ilg, 2008; de Hemptinne et al., 2006; Kowler et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The population average of FEFSEM firing across the full sample of neurons was strongly tuned to the direction of target motion and pursuit.
source: The population average of FEFSEM firing across our full sample of neurons was strongly tuned to the direction of target motion and pursuit (Figure 5B), with a large increase in firing rate in the 'preferred direction' of the cell, a smaller increase when motion was at +/- 45 degrees from the preferred direction, no modulation for visual motion orthogonal to the preferred direction, and decreases in firing rate for +/- 135 degrees and 180 degrees from the preferred direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the neural data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The optimal linear model assigned a continuous distribution of weight magnitudes to the members of the FEFSEM population.
source: Our fitting procedure assigned a continuous distribution of weight magnitudes to the members of our population (Figure 5C), showing that the model used the entire FEFSEM population and did not simply pick out a few particularly informative cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The optimal linear model produced fairly accurate predictions for horizontal eye velocity.
source: The model worked well on data from pursuit trials that were not used to compute the weights: target motion at three different speeds (2, 10, and 20 deg/s) and two different contrasts (12% and 100%) from a separate block of trials that presented visual motion in a single, repeated direction. It produced fairly accurate predictions for horizontal eye velocity (Figure 5D, slope = 1.09, r2 = 0.85) and accurately predicted zero vertical eye velocities (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cross-validation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The optimal linear model accurately predicted zero vertical eye velocities.
source: It produced fairly accurate predictions for horizontal eye velocity (Figure 5D, slope = 1.09, r2 = 0.85) and accurately predicted zero vertical eye velocities (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text but the supporting data is not shown.

claim: FEFSEM preparatory activity does not avoid movement-potent neural dimensions.
source: FEFSEM preparatory activity does not avoid movement-potent neural dimensions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the optimal linear model analysis shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The optimal linear model predicts movement when there is none, during fixation and preparatory activity.
source: The optimal linear model predicts movement when there is none, during fixation and preparatory activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The output of the linear model predicts eye movement in a direction that is appropriate for the upcoming target motion.
source: Importantly, the output of the linear model predicts eye movement in a direction that is appropriate for the upcoming target motion according to how neurons across experimental sessions were combined into a pseudo-population (see below): a large positive horizontal component and relatively smaller vertical component.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The single trial analysis predicts non-zero eye velocity with a significant projection in the direction of the subsequent pursuit trial.
source: Consistent with the findings of Figure 6A and B, the single trial analysis predicts non-zero eye velocity with a significant projection in the direction of the subsequent pursuit trial (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-trial bootstrap analysis shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: The mean predicted direction from the single trial analysis was −1.3 deg with a 95% bootstrap interval of −65.8 to +71.8 deg.
source: The mean predicted direction was −1.3 deg with a 95% bootstrap interval of −65.8 to +71.8 deg; the mean predicted eye speed was 2.9 deg/s.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-trial bootstrap analysis.

claim: The mean predicted eye speed from the single trial analysis was 2.9 deg/s.
source: The mean predicted direction was −1.3 deg with a 95% bootstrap interval of −65.8 to +71.8 deg; the mean predicted eye speed was 2.9 deg/s.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-trial bootstrap analysis.

claim: For the motor system studied here, the data do not fulfill one important prediction of the null-space hypothesis: the optimal linear model for pursuit initiation predicts significant non-zero eye velocities driven by preparatory activity.
source: Thus, for the motor system we study, the data do not fulfill one important prediction of the null-space hypothesis: the optimal linear model for pursuit initiation predicts significant non-zero eye velocities driven by preparatory activity.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the optimal linear model analysis.

claim: The first preparatory and pursuit PCs each capture more than 70% of the variance.
source: After reducing the dimensionality of our preparatory- and pursuit-related population responses during the single-direction trial blocks, we analyze the first preparatory and pursuit PCs (PCPrep1 and PCPurs1), each of which captures more than 70% of the variance (Figure 7A), the same amount captured by the dimensionality reduction in Elsayed et al. (2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The projection of pursuit-related activity onto PCPurs1 captures differences in both the speed of target motion and the contrast of the target.
source: We validated PCPurs1 by showing that the projection of pursuit-related activity onto the PCPurs1 captures differences in both the speed of target motion and the contrast of the target: in parallel with the neural responses, the projections scaled with target speed and are larger in magnitude and shorter in latency for high- compared to low-contrast targets (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The projection of preparatory activity onto PCPurs1 shows a ramp increase across fixation.
source: As expected, given the results in the previous section using the optimal linear model, the projection of preparatory activity onto PCPurs1 shows a ramp increase across fixation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The main difference between the preparatory and pursuit projections is that the preparatory projection ramps up more slowly to a smaller magnitude compared to the pursuit projections.
source: The main difference between the preparatory and pursuit projections is that the preparatory projection ramps up more slowly to a smaller magnitude compared to the pursuit projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing the projections shown in Figure 7B and 7D.

claim: The mean angle between PCPrep1 and PCPurs1 is 65.2 degrees and is significantly different from both 0 and 90.
source: We find that the mean angle between PCPrep1 and PCPurs1 is 65.2 degrees and is significantly different from both 0 and 90 (Figure 7C, p<0.001, two-sided bootstrap statistics, 95% bootstrap interval = 61.4–69.2 deg, n = 1000 iterations).
evidence: This claim is supported by the bootstrap analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Preparatory- and pursuit-related neural dimensions are neither aligned nor completely orthogonal in the population of FEFSEM neurons.
source: Therefore, preparatory- and pursuit-related neural dimensions are neither aligned nor completely orthogonal in our population of FEFSEM neurons.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the PCA analysis showing the angle between PCPrep1 and PCPurs1 is 65.2 degrees.

claim: The distribution of the ratios between the PCA component loadings of PCPrep1 and PCPurs1 is significantly bimodal.
source: The distribution of the ratios between the PCA component loadings of PCPrep1 and PCPurs1, generated from the bootstrap in Figure 3B, is significantly bimodal (Figure 8A, Hartigan's Dip Test, Dip statistic = 0.0794, p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the distribution shown in Figure 8A.

claim: A positive PCPrep1/PCPurs1 ratio indicates that a given unit behaves in a similar manner during preparation and movement.
source: A positive ratio indicates that a given unit behaves in a similar manner during preparation and movement, whereas a negative ratio indicates a change in behavior between preparation and pursuit.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the meaning of the ratio values.

claim: A negative PCPrep1/PCPurs1 ratio indicates a change in behavior between preparation and pursuit.
source: A positive ratio indicates that a given unit behaves in a similar manner during preparation and movement, whereas a negative ratio indicates a change in behavior between preparation and pursuit.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the meaning of the ratio values.

claim: There are two subpopulations in FEFSEM, and the one with negative PCPrep1/PCPurs1 ratios may be responsible for the partial reorganization of population activity between preparation and movement.
source: We conclude that there are two subpopulations in FEFSEM, and that the one with negative PCPrep1/PCPurs1 ratios may be responsible for the partial reorganization of population activity between preparation and movement.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the bimodal distribution of PCPrep1/PCPurs1 ratios.

claim: Subpopulation 1 consistently made up a larger proportion of units in the bootstrap analysis and contains a higher proportion of units with a preferred direction towards the direction of the single-direction experiment.
source: Subpopulation 1 consistently made up a larger proportion of units in our bootstrap analysis and contains a higher proportion of units with a preferred direction towards the direction of the single-direction experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the bootstrap analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Subpopulation 2 contains a higher proportion of units with preferred directions away from the direction of the experiment.
source: Conversely, Subpopulation 2 contains a higher proportion of units with preferred directions away from the direction of the experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the bootstrap analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Neurons in Subpopulation 1 had statistically larger amplitudes of both preparatory- and pursuit-related modulation compared to Subpopulation 2.
source: When we redid principal component analysis on the full (non-bootstrapped) data, neurons in Subpopulation 1 had statistically larger amplitudes of both preparatory- and pursuit-related modulation (compare red and black data points in Figure 8C; preparatory activity: p=0.019, Cohen's d = 0.34, pursuit activity: p=2.7×10−12, Cohen's d = 0.95, 2-sided Wilcoxon rank sum tests).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between preparatory and pursuit modulation in Subpopulation 1.
source: There is a significant positive correlation between preparatory and pursuit modulation in Subpopulation 1 (Figure 8C, Spearman's correlation coefficient = 0.59, p=7.8×10−21, n = 207 samples from 130 neurons) and a significant negative correlation in Subpopulation 2 (Figure 8C, Spearman's correlation coefficient = −0.63, p=3.8×10−11, n = 90 samples from 65 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between preparatory and pursuit modulation in Subpopulation 2.
source: There is a significant positive correlation between preparatory and pursuit modulation in Subpopulation 1 (Figure 8C, Spearman's correlation coefficient = 0.59, p=7.8×10−21, n = 207 samples from 130 neurons) and a significant negative correlation in Subpopulation 2 (Figure 8C, Spearman's correlation coefficient = −0.63, p=3.8×10−11, n = 90 samples from 65 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: For Subpopulation 1 alone, the first principal components of pursuit and preparatory activity are separated by an angle of only 26.2 degrees.
source: For Subpopulation 1 alone, the first principal components of pursuit and preparatory activity are separated by an angle of only 26.2 degrees.
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 8G.

claim: For Subpopulation 2 alone, the angle between PCPrep1 and PCPurs1 is 151.2 degrees.
source: For Subpopulation 2 alone, the angle between PCPrep1 and PCPurs1 is 151.2 degrees (Figure 8G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Subpopulation 2 is responsible for the partial reorganization of population activity between preparation and movement.
source: These facts suggest that Subpopulation 2 is responsible for the partial reorganization of population activity between preparation and movement, and that the large difference in response amplitudes between the two populations is at least partly responsible for a lack of full reorganization between preparatory- and movement-related dimensions.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the differences in angles between PCPrep1 and PCPurs1 for the two subpopulations.

claim: The large difference in response amplitudes between the two populations is at least partly responsible for a lack of full reorganization between preparatory- and movement-related dimensions.
source: These facts suggest that Subpopulation 2 is responsible for the partial reorganization of population activity between preparation and movement, and that the large difference in response amplitudes between the two populations is at least partly responsible for a lack of full reorganization between preparatory- and movement-related dimensions.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of the two subpopulations.

claim: In Subpopulation 1, preparatory modulation of firing rate has conventional direction tuning.
source: In Subpopulation 1, preparatory modulation of firing rate has conventional direction tuning. It is large and positive when the upcoming target motion will be in the preferred direction of the cell, smaller when it will be orthogonal to the preferred direction, and negative when it will be opposite to the preferred direction of the cell (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8D and 8E.

claim: In Subpopulation 2, preparatory modulation of firing rate has weaker and non-conventional direction tuning.
source: In Subpopulation 2, preparatory modulation of firing rate has weaker and non-conventional direction tuning. Modulation is positive when the upcoming target motion is orthogonal or opposite to the preferred direction and absent when target motion will be toward the preferred direction (Figure 8D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8D and 8F.

claim: The preparatory activity in Subpopulation 1 explains why preparatory enhancement of visual-motor gain is largest in the direction of the upcoming target motion.
source: Together, the two subpopulations can explain two features of Figure 4A. The preparatory activity in Subpopulation 1 explains why preparatory enhancement of visual-motor gain is largest in the direction of the upcoming target motion.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation linking the neural properties of Subpopulation 1 to the behavioral findings.

claim: The smaller preparatory activity in Subpopulation 2 might explain the directionally-nonspecific, and smaller, component of preparatory visual-motor gain enhancement in orthogonal and opposite directions relative to the upcoming target motion.
source: The smaller preparatory activity in Subpopulation 2 might explain the directionally-nonspecific, and smaller, component of preparatory visual-motor gain enhancement in orthogonal and opposite directions relative to the upcoming target motion.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation linking the neural properties of Subpopulation 2 to the behavioral findings.

claim: Linear models generated from the two subpopulations perform roughly the same in predicting eye velocity during the single direction block.
source: To further examine differences between the two subpopulations, we repeated the optimal linear model analysis from Figures 5 and 6 separately on each subpopulation. Linear models generated from the two subpopulations perform roughly the same in predicting eye velocity during the single direction block (Figure 9A,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 9A and 9D.

claim: Subpopulation 1 predicts eye movement during preparation in the same direction as the upcoming visual motion and eye movement.
source: Subpopulation 1 predicts eye movement during preparation in the same direction as the upcoming visual motion and eye movement (Figure 9B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 9B and 9C.

claim: Subpopulation 2 predicts no significant eye movement during preparation.
source: Subpopulation 2 predicts no significant eye movement during preparation (Figure 9E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 9E and 9F.

claim: The nonspecific component of visual-motor gain is fairly uniform across directions.
source: However, it is worth pointing out that the spread around zero for horizontal and vertical eye velocities is quite large. These features are consistent with Subpopulation 2 dialing up visual-motor gain in a directionally-nonspecific manner and they suggest that the nonspecific component of visual-motor gain is fairly uniform across directions.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the analysis shown in Figure 9E and 9F.

claim: Preparatory activity is an important component of voluntary movement.
source: Preparation is an important component of voluntary movement.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the extensive literature cited in the introduction.

claim: Throughout the motor system, many neurons show modulation of firing rate that occurs during movement preparation and is linked to parameters of the ensuing movement.
source: Throughout the motor system, many neurons show modulation of firing rate that occurs during movement preparation and is linked to parameters of the ensuing movement (Dorris et al., 1997; Glimcher and Sparks, 1992; Hanes and Schall, 1996; Munoz and Wurtz, 1995; Tanaka and Fukushima, 1998; Tanji and Evarts, 1976; Weinrich and Wise, 1982; Wurtz and Goldberg, 1972; Churchland et al., 2006a; Churchland et al., 2006b; Darlington et al., 2018; Hanes and Schall, 1996; Mahaffy and Krauzlis, 2011; Messier and Kalaska, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to prior work across multiple motor systems.

claim: Many neurons that seem to be tied to movement still have preparatory activity, even though there is neither movement nor muscle activity during preparation.
source: Importantly, many neurons that seem to be tied to movement still have preparatory activity, even though there is neither movement nor muscle activity during preparation.
evidence: This is a general observation supported by the literature and the current data.

claim: Motor and premotor cells in the cerebral cortex and even the brainstem and spinal cord show preparatory activity without causing inappropriate movement.
source: How can motor and premotor cells in the cerebral cortex and even the brainstem and spinal cord (Glimcher and Sparks, 1992; Munoz and Wurtz, 1995; Prut and Fetz, 1999) show preparatory activity without causing inappropriate movement?
evidence: This is a question posed based on observations supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The discharge of the neurons involved in the switch for saccades is incompatible with the idea that pursuit might use the same switch circuit.
source: The discharge of the neurons involved in the switch for saccades is incompatible with the idea that pursuit might use the same switch circuit (Missal and Keller, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The firing of omnipause neurons pauses completely during the execution of saccades of any direction and amplitude but exhibits directionally-tuned decrements of firing rate that are graded according to eye speed during smooth pursuit eye movement.
source: The firing of omnipause neurons pauses completely during the execution of saccades of any direction and amplitude but exhibits directionally-tuned decrements of firing rate that are graded according to eye speed during smooth pursuit eye movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by the context of the discussion and citations to prior work.

claim: It is possible that FEFSEM output interacts with omnipause neurons.
source: Indeed, it is possible that FEFSEM output interacts with omnipause neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on anatomical and functional considerations.

claim: Omnipause neurons are anatomically connected to at least the saccadic frontal eye fields.
source: Omnipause neurons are anatomically connected to at least the saccadic frontal eye fields and their responses during pursuit align closely with properties of visual-motor gain (Langer and Kaneko, 1990; Missal and Keller, 2002; Schwartz and Lisberger, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The responses of omnipause neurons during pursuit align closely with properties of visual-motor gain.
source: Omnipause neurons are anatomically connected to at least the saccadic frontal eye fields and their responses during pursuit align closely with properties of visual-motor gain (Langer and Kaneko, 1990; Missal and Keller, 2002; Schwartz and Lisberger, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Lesioning and inactivating FEFSEM results in large decrements of pursuit speed and an increase in the number of catch-up saccades.
source: Lesioning and inactivating FEFSEM results in large decrements of pursuit speed and an increase in the number of catch-up saccades (Keating, 1991; Shi et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The output of FEFSEM (and possibly partner areas such as the Supplementary Eye Fields) is necessary to allow visual motion signals to drive the oculomotor machinery.
source: The output of FEFSEM (and possibly partner areas such as the Supplementary Eye Fields Missal and Heinen, 2001) is necessary to allow visual motion signals to drive the oculomotor machinery (Tanaka and Lisberger, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There are trial-by-trial correlations between FEFSEM activity during pursuit and eye velocity.
source: Furthermore, there are trial-by-trial correlations between FEFSEM activity during pursuit and eye velocity (Schoppik et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The artificial situation created by micro-stimulation will drive activity in brainstem oculomotor neurons simply because FEFSEM is anatomically connected to the motor system.
source: We suspect that the artificial situation created by micro-stimulation will drive activity in brainstem oculomotor neurons simply because FEFSEM is anatomically connected to the motor system.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of microstimulation results.

claim: Micro-stimulation-generated smooth eye movements may say little about how FEFSEM output is actually used downstream.
source: Beyond general anatomical connectivity, micro-stimulation-generated smooth eye movements may say little about how FEFSEM output is actually used downstream.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of microstimulation results.

claim: The brain uses multiple mechanisms to prevent preparatory activity from causing unwanted and premature movement.
source: We suggest that the brain uses multiple mechanisms to prevent preparatory activity from causing unwanted and premature movement, and that the primary mechanism used by any particular movement system will depend on the organization of that particular system.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the discussion of different motor systems.

claim: The primary mechanism used by any particular movement system to prevent preparatory activity from causing movement will depend on the organization of that particular system.
source: We suggest that the brain uses multiple mechanisms to prevent preparatory activity from causing unwanted and premature movement, and that the primary mechanism used by any particular movement system will depend on the organization of that particular system.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the discussion of different motor systems.

claim: A system could use multiple mechanisms at the same time to prevent preparatory activity from causing movement, perhaps emphasizing one or another.
source: Further, a system could use multiple mechanisms at the same time, perhaps emphasizing one or another.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about how motor systems might operate.

claim: In pursuit, movement initiation is driven directly, with relatively short latencies, by sensory inputs from extrastriate visual area MT.
source: In pursuit, movement initiation is driven directly, with relatively short latencies, by sensory inputs from extrastriate visual area MT (Komatsu and Wurtz, 1989; Newsome et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Outputs from MT and FEFSEM converge downstream in the pursuit circuit to control the activity of motoneurons.
source: Outputs from MT and FEFSEM converge downstream in the pursuit circuit to control the activity of motoneurons (Lisberger, 2010; Mustari et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Preparatory modulation of visual-motor gain is a genuine preparatory signal.
source: Importantly, preparatory modulation of visual-motor gain is a genuine preparatory signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data showing that preparatory activity encodes expected target parameters.

claim: FEFSEM preparatory responses encode the expected speed and direction of the upcoming target motion.
source: FEFSEM preparatory responses encode the expected speed and direction of the upcoming target motion and FEFSEM seems to set the state of the pursuit system during preparation in a way that sculpts the subsequent visual motion signals (Darlington et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and the current data.

claim: FEFSEM seems to set the state of the pursuit system during preparation in a way that sculpts the subsequent visual motion signals.
source: FEFSEM preparatory responses encode the expected speed and direction of the upcoming target motion and FEFSEM seems to set the state of the pursuit system during preparation in a way that sculpts the subsequent visual motion signals (Darlington et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and the current data.

claim: In the arm movement system and the motor cortex, it may be difficult to prevent activity in the motor cortex from affecting the firing of motoneurons.
source: In the arm movement system and the motor cortex, it may be difficult to prevent activity in the motor cortex from affecting the firing of motoneurons, and so it is ideal to nullify the preparatory activity by contriving for it to reside in a movement-null dimension.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why the arm movement system might use movement-null dimensions.

claim: The link from sensory input to motor output is less direct for arm movements than for pursuit.
source: Here, the link from sensory input to motor output is less direct than for pursuit and the output from the primary motor cortex and the premotor cortex affect the firing of motoneurons directly, over monosynaptic and disynaptic pathways (Dum and Strick, 1991; Griffin et al., 2015; Kuypers and Brinkman, 1970).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the anatomy of the arm movement system.

claim: The output from the primary motor cortex and the premotor cortex affect the firing of motoneurons directly, over monosynaptic and disynaptic pathways.
source: Here, the link from sensory input to motor output is less direct than for pursuit and the output from the primary motor cortex and the premotor cortex affect the firing of motoneurons directly, over monosynaptic and disynaptic pathways (Dum and Strick, 1991; Griffin et al., 2015; Kuypers and Brinkman, 1970).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the anatomy of the arm movement system.

claim: It is possible that gain control mechanisms also operate in arm movements, both to implement the essential function of adjusting to different contexts, and to allow preparatory activity without movement.
source: That said, it is possible that gain control mechanisms also operate in arm movements, both to implement the essential function of adjusting to different contexts, and to allow preparatory activity without movement.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms in the arm movement system.

claim: Recent work in the mouse motor system revealed subpopulations of motor cortex neurons with distinct roles in preparation and movement.
source: Just as we think that FEFSEM is responsible for the preparatory aspects of pursuit and area MT is responsible for the movement drive, recent work in the mouse motor system revealed subpopulations of motor cortex neurons with distinct roles in preparation and movement (Economo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Last-order interneurons in the spinal cord show arm-movement-related preparatory activity that could reflect motor cortical modulation of the gain of spinal reflex circuits.
source: Furthermore, last-order interneurons in the spinal cord show arm-movement-related preparatory activity that could reflect motor cortical modulation of the gain of spinal reflex circuits (Prut and Fetz, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and is a speculative interpretation.

claim: In saccadic eye movements, the need for high degrees of accuracy and precision in a totally open-loop movement probably requires the preparatory activity that exists at least in the frontal eye fields, the superior colliculus, and the parietal cortex.
source: In saccadic eye movements, the need for high degrees of accuracy and precision in a totally open-loop movement probably requires the preparatory activity that exists at least in the frontal eye fields, the superior colliculus, and the parietal cortex, but also requires an absolute brake on movement until all the brain's ducks are in a row (Glimcher and Sparks, 1992; Hanes and Schall, 1996; Mazzoni et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why the saccadic system uses a switching mechanism, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The switching circuit in the brainstem prevents any movement until the activity that guides the direction and amplitude of the impending saccade is fully prepared to make a movement that is at the same time really quick and accurate.
source: Here, the switching circuit in the brainstem prevents any movement until the activity that guides the direction and amplitude of the impending saccade is fully prepared to make a movement that is at the same time really quick and accurate (Robinson, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on the saccadic system.

claim: A monkey executes a 20 deg saccade in 40 ms with accuracy of better than 5%.
source: For example, a monkey executes a 20 deg saccade in 40 ms with accuracy of better than 5% (Fuchs, 1967).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Pursuit eye movements are much slower and less accurate than saccades.
source: By contrast, pursuit eye movements are much slower and less accurate, and arm movements rely partly on feedback to achieve maximum accuracy.
evidence: This is a general statement based on knowledge of motor systems.

claim: Arm movements rely partly on feedback to achieve maximum accuracy.
source: By contrast, pursuit eye movements are much slower and less accurate, and arm movements rely partly on feedback to achieve maximum accuracy.
evidence: This is a general statement based on knowledge of motor systems.

claim: A switching circuit could exist for movements other than saccades, perhaps in a softer, more compliant form.
source: A switching circuit could exist for movements other than saccades, perhaps in a softer, more compliant form.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms in other motor systems.

claim: Gain control may be an ideal way to establish context sensitivity and adjust the responsiveness to descending signals in systems with short latencies and graded responses.
source: Gain control, may be an ideal way to establish context sensitivity and adjust the responsiveness to descending signals in systems with short latencies and graded responses.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the current findings.

claim: The dynamical system regime may be specialized for neural systems where the neurons involved in preparation make synaptic connections directly onto final motor pathways.
source: The dynamical system regime may be specialized for neural systems where the neurons involved in preparation make synaptic connections directly onto final motor pathways.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about when the dynamical system mechanism might be most useful.

claim: Two male rhesus monkeys aged 8–10 years and weighing between 12 and 14 kg were used in the neurophysiology experiments.
source: As described in Darlington et al. (2018), two male rhesus monkeys aged 8–10 years and weighing between 12 and 14 kg were used in the neurophysiology experiments (Darlington et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The same two monkeys used in the neurophysiology experiments were used for the new behavioral experiments.
source: The same two monkeys were used for the new behavioral experiments presented here.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

source: All procedures received prior approval by Duke's Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and complied with the National Institutes of Health's Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
